title: Quantum ring all-reduce: communication and privacy advantages for distributed learning
abstract: Machine learning models have scaled to unprecedented sizes, making training across distributed devices the de facto standard in the field. In this work, we explore how quantum communications can make distributed training both more communication-efficient and information-theoretically private, for both classical and quantum learning models. Ring all-reduce is the foundational communication primitive for large-scale distributed training. We present a quantum version that reduces per-link online communication by a provably optimal factor of two using pre-shared entanglement and superdense coding, without requiring the learning model or gradient computation to change. Beyond bandwidth, the primitive enables privacy guarantees that are information-theoretically impossible for any classical protocol, achieving composable ε-secure aggregation, via verified entanglement, at a 2x overhead in GHZ copies. Our hybrid quantum-classical communication architecture yields simultaneous communication and security advantages for large scale distributed training, regardless of whether the learning itself is quantum or classical. Finally, we characterise quantum advantages in gradient conflict detection for server-to-client communication under bandwidth constraints, a setting that arises after ring all-reduce is completed, when full gradient broadcast to external clients is infeasible. Two variants of the problem admit different separations. For margin-based alignment testing (\textsc{GapIP}_τ), the quantum advantage is quadratic in the margin parameter: \widetilde{O}(τ^{-1}\log P) qubits versus \widetilde{O}(\min(\τ^{-2},P)) bits. For sign-consistency auditing against a private parameter matching (\textsc{TieAudit}_ε), the advantage represents an exponential separation in communication complexity: Ω(\sqrt{P}) bits whereas O(ε^{-2}\log P) qubits suffice.
summary: This work develops a quantum enhancement for the ring all-reduce primitive used in distributed machine learning. It demonstrates that quantum resources provide provable advantages by halving online communication costs and enabling information-theoretic privacy guarantees unattainable classically. Furthermore, it establishes exponential quantum separations when detecting gradient conflicts.
main_problem: To enhance distributed machine learning training by making the foundational communication primitive, ring all-reduce, both more communication-efficient and information-theoretically private using quantum communications.
main_result: The authors present a quantum ring all-reduce protocol that achieves a provably optimal factor of two reduction in online communication via superdense coding and enables privacy guarantees impossible classically through Verified GHZ Aggregation (VGA).
method: The work combines techniques like pre-shared entanglement, superdense coding for bandwidth savings, and encoding gradients into the phases of shared GHZ states to achieve security proofs.
model_or_system: The core model is the quantum ring all-reduce primitive applied to $N$ workers holding local gradients. The analysis uses concepts from communication complexity, including comparing classical bit requirements against qubit resources derived from entanglement and GHZ states.
key_observables: Communication cost (qubits vs. bits), information leakage ($I(g_j; V_E)$), Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$), and the separation factors for conflict detection tasks ($	ext{GapIP}_	au$ and $	ext{TieAudit}_\epsilon$).
important_parameters: The number of workers $N$, the gradient dimension $P$, the privacy error $\epsilon$, and the margin threshold $	au$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the availability of pre-shared entanglement (EPR pairs) and relies on asymptotic bounds for security proofs, requiring finite-key corrections for practical deployment.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the superdense-coding protocol for $N=3$ workers, detailing both classical bit costs and quantum qubit costs across different rounds of the all-reduce process.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing bandwidth savings via superdense coding in the ring all-reduce. It then introduces VGA for information-theoretic privacy guarantees. Finally, it analyzes two specific conflict detection tasks ($	ext{GapIP}_	au$ and $	ext{TieAudit}_\epsilon$) to demonstrate exponential quantum advantages.
why_interesting: The paper provides a rigorous framework showing how fundamental quantum communication primitives (like entanglement assistance) can solve resource limitations in large-scale computation, which is highly relevant for understanding the limits of distributed quantum algorithms.
